findings.title: Private-binding guard is a denylist; a new AzureAISearchConfig option is web-authorable by default
findings.summary: author_names is every property minus AZURE_AI_SEARCH_PRIVATE_BINDING_OPTION_NAMES, and lower_options spreads author options next to the operator's endpoint and injected credential (line 1321). The comment at 1220-1222 records this as deliberate ('Computed, not listed'), and recent-code-hints.md has no ruling on it. I think the design is wrong here: a binding-shaped field that is not added to the private set fails open. The Textract precedent uses a positive allowlist (TEXTRACT_PROFILED_AUTHOR_OPTION_NAMES). Tests pin only the private set (test_ai_search.py:84-88) and a subset relation (test_profiles.py:579-580).
findings.failure_scenario: A later change adds a binding-shaped option to AzureAISearchConfig, such as auth_mode, a token scope, or a proxy or endpoint override. It becomes authorable in web pipelines and is lowered next to the operator's server credential with no web-tier edit or failing test. A web author can then alter a request that carries the deployment's credential.
findings.evidence: profiles.py:1220-1223 (subtraction and design comment), 1316 (private-name refusal), 1321 (executable = {**safe_options, endpoint}); tests assert only a subset relation (test_profiles.py:579-580) and the private set's exact membership (test_ai_search.py:84-88); no ruling found by grep of recent-code-hints.md.
findings.suggested_fix: Pin the author-visible set exactly, for example with a test asserting AzureAISearchConfig.model_fields minus PRIVATE equals a reviewed tuple, or switch to a positive allowlist as Textract does.

verdicts.reason: The finding describes no failure at the pinned commit. Its failure scenario depends on "a later change adds a binding-shaped option", and nothing in the tree today reaches that state. I checked every current AzureAISearchConfig field. Each one is either in the private set or is ordinary query or row-mapping configuration. The five binding options (endpoint, api_key, use_managed_identity, client_id, api_version) are all in AZURE_AI_SEARCH_PRIVATE_BINDING_OPTION_NAMES. That set is removed from the published schema (profiles.py:1223). lower_options refuses those names before it adds the endpoint and credential (profiles.py:1316, then 1321). So a web author cannot change a request that carries the operator's credential today. The subtraction design was also chosen on purpose, in writing, in two places. Commit d3dba8a9b says: "The author-visible option set is computed ... a new binding option must join the private set to be hidden". The approved plan says the same (docs/plans/2026-09-20-azure-ai-search-plugin.md:860). The reviewer rightly notes that recent-code-hints.md has no ruling. What remains is a design preference: an allowlist, as Textract uses, instead of a denylist. That makes it a hardening suggestion, not a confirmed defect. The reviewer is right on one minor point: the commit message says "which the tests pin", but the tests only pin the private set's exact membership and that each private name is a real option. No test would catch a new binding-shaped field that someone forgets to add to the set.

findings.title: Contract comment claims the private set is shared with the plugin; the plugin does not use it
findings.summary: The module comment says 'Shared by the plugin and the web policy layer so the two cannot drift', but only web/plugin_policy/profiles.py imports AZURE_AI_SEARCH_PRIVATE_BINDING_OPTION_NAMES. plugins/transforms/azure/ai_search.py does not; only its unit test does.
findings.failure_scenario: A maintainer trusts the comment and assumes the plugin enforces or derives from the split. They add a binding option to the plugin without touching the contract, expecting the shared constant to keep both sides aligned. The web tier then silently exposes the new option (see F1).
findings.evidence: grep -rn AZURE_AI_SEARCH_PRIVATE_BINDING_OPTION_NAMES src/ -> contracts/azure_ai_search.py:5 and web/plugin_policy/profiles.py:31,1223,1316 only.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to say the web policy layer owns the set and the plugin's test pins it to real options, or have the plugin actually derive something from it.

verdicts.reason:
The factual core holds at 74c0ce0db. src/elspeth/contracts/azure_ai_search.py:3-4 says the set is "Shared by the plugin and the web policy layer so the two cannot drift". No production plugin code reads it. The only source consumer is web/plugin_policy/profiles.py (import at :31, used at :1223 and :1316). src/elspeth/plugins/transforms/azure/ai_search.py never imports it; the plugin marks itself operator-bound only through `web_config_authority = WebConfigAuthority.OPERATOR_PROFILED` (ai_search.py:90-92). So "shared by the plugin" is imprecise: the thing that shares it is the plugin's unit test, not the plugin.

The finding overstates the harm, though. The comment's "cannot drift" claim is partly backed by that test. tests/unit/plugins/transforms/azure/test_ai_search.py:82-88 checks that every private name is a real field of AzureAISearchConfig, and that the set exactly matches a literal list. Renaming or removing a private option therefore fails a test, so that direction of drift is guarded. The failure scenario the reviewer gives (a new sensitive option added to the plugin that the web tier then exposes) is the other direction. An accurate comment would not prevent it, because the plugin has nothing it could derive privacy from. That risk belongs to F1, not to this comment. What remains is a misleading comment with no runtime effect: low severity, close to a documentation nit, but not wrong.

grep -rn AZURE_AI_SEARCH_PRIVATE_BINDING_OPTION_NAMES over src/ and tests/ in the worktree:

Pinning test, test_ai_search.py:82-88:
`assert set(AzureAISearchConfig.model_fields) >= AZURE_AI_SEARCH_PRIVATE_BINDING_OPTION_NAMES`, plus an exact-equality check against the literal {endpoint, api_key, use_managed_identity, client_id, api_version}. This covers rename/remove drift, but not a new option that is never classified.

findings.title: Profiled example_use hard-codes index 'approved-documents' regardless of the operator's pins
findings.summary: public_summary's azure arm teaches 'index: approved-documents' whatever indexes the available profiles admit. That undercuts the design promise that the public schema tells the planner the admitted indexes 'so it never guesses a name'.
findings.failure_scenario: Two usable profiles, hr pinned to ['hr-records'] and legal pinned to ['contracts'], so there is no index enum. The planner copies the example index, and lowering refuses the node with profile_index_not_admitted ('Index is not admitted by the selected Azure AI Search profile'). The author spends a repair turn.
findings.evidence: profiles.py:1602-1621 (example_use literal); design doc §3 'so it never guesses a name'; index enum is only published for a single closed pin (profiles.py:1244-1250).
findings.suggested_fix: Derive the example index from the sole closed pin when there is one; otherwise use an obvious placeholder such as <an index the profile lists>.

verdicts.reason: The literal is real: profiles.py:1617 hard-codes `index: approved-documents` in the azure arm's example_use. But the claim that this undercuts the design promise misreads how the promise is kept. The design doc (docs/plans/2026-09-20-azure-search-retrieval-plugin-design.md:124-127) says the planner learns the admitted indexes in one of two ways: an `index` enum when one alias is usable, and per-alias lists in the `profile` description otherwise. The worked example is not one of those channels. The code does both. In the multi-profile case the reviewer describes, public_summary builds config_fields from the same public_schema (profiles.py:1542-1559). The `profile` field description in that summary reads "Operator-approved Azure AI Search profile alias. Indexes each profile admits: hr: hr-records; legal: contracts" (profiles.py:1222-1224). So the list the planner needs sits in the same payload as the example. A test pins this: test_profiles.py:591-596. The example's placeholder style also matches the sibling arms: S3 uses the literal `key: records/input.csv` (profiles.py:1585) and Textract uses the literal `key_field: document_key`. The base plugin's own example uses the same literal (plugins/transforms/azure/ai_search.py:113). The failure scenario only happens if the LLM copies an illustrative example over an explicit admitted-index list it has in the same message. That is a guess about model behaviour, not a code path I could trace. Even then, the path recovers cleanly: lowering refuses with a value-free, actionable message, "choose an index the profile lists" (validation.py:545-550), and the adjacent profile description names the lists. At most this is a teaching-polish nit: the example could use a placeholder or derive the index from a sole closed pin. It is not a confirmed defect.
verdicts.evidence: profiles.py:1617 is the `index: approved-documents` literal. profiles.py:1222-1224 builds profile_description = "... Indexes each profile admits: " followed by the per-alias pins. profiles.py:1225-1231 and 1284-1291 put that description on the `profile` property and knob. profiles.py:1242-1247 sets the index enum only for a single closed pin, as designed. profiles.py:1542-1559 shows that public_summary derives config_fields (including the profile description) from resolver.public_schema, so the list travels in the same summary as example_use. design doc 2026-09-20-azure-search-retrieval-plugin-design.md:124-127 names exactly those two channels ("per-alias lists in the `profile` description otherwise"). tests/unit/web/plugin_policy/test_profiles.py:591-596 asserts "policies: approved-documents" and "contracts: any index" appear in the description. validation.py:545-550 gives the recoverable message "choose an index the profile lists". The sibling examples use placeholder literals too (profiles.py:1585, 1597; ai_search.py:113).

findings.title: Administrator account creation and password reset have no Landscape audit row; the surface now reaches every local-auth administrator
findings.summary: ce3602aed removed the docstring that justified structlog-only records ('this surface is off in any deployment whose audit trail matters'). It also enabled create_user and reset_password for every active human admin on local-auth deployments. Both still emit only _slog.info, and the auth audit recorder has no event for either.
findings.failure_scenario: On a local-auth deployment, admin A POSTs /api/auth/admin/users/B/reset-password, receives B's new password and signs in as B. The Landscape auth audit shows only B's login. No durable row records that A reset B's credential, so the evidence exists only in ephemeral logs, which the audit-primacy policy forbids for probative events.
findings.evidence: admin_routes.py:1-10 docstring rewritten in ce3602aed. admin_routes.py:203 and :220 are _slog.info only. local.py:451 create_user and :720 set_password write no audit. web/auth/audit.py record_* has no credential-created or password-reset event. Deletion is audited through local_identity_retirer. No ruling in recent-code-hints.md or the people-access plan docs.
findings.suggested_fix: Add auth-audit events for administrator credential creation and reset (actor identity_id, target username, no secret material), recorded before the password is returned. Otherwise restore the gating that justified structlog-only records.

verdicts.reason: I could not refute this finding; the path is reachable exactly as described. At the pinned commit, `_require_local_account_admin` (admin_routes.py:145-157) admits any caller on a local-auth deployment whose identity_id is in `RepositoryIdentityAuthority.active_human_admin_ids()` (identity_authority.py:1471-1482), or the configured dev_admin_user. Before ce3602aed only the dev_admin_user could get in. Once admitted, `create_user` (admin_routes.py:184-205) and `reset_password` (admin_routes.py:207-222) write to auth.db through `LocalAuthProvider.create_user` (local.py:451-481) and `set_password` (local.py:720-735). Neither method writes an audit row, and the routes emit only `_slog.info` (lines 203 and 220). The Web auth recorder (web/auth/audit.py) has record_* methods for login, token, identity admitted/retired/rebound/enabled/disabled/activated, role, relationship, quota, approval, review and library events, but none for credential creation or password reset. There is no guard that stops one admin resetting another admin's password. Only two commits in the window touch admin_routes.py and audit.py (ce3602aed and 793d0f95a), and neither adds an audit event. The 'structlog-only' choice was a recorded design decision only while the surface was dev-only. The SSO spec (docs/specs/2026-09-02-pluggable-sso-design.md:969) says 'the existing dev-admin gate is local-only and structlog-only by design', and the old docstring and the old config.py comment both said the surface was for short-term dev deployments and off wherever the audit trail matters. ce3602aed removed both premises and widened the surface to every local-auth administrator. The new docstring line 'Credential creation and reset retain their operational log events' states what the code does but is not a ruling. I found nothing in recent-code-hints.md or the people-access plan or review docs that re-justifies structlog-only records for the wider population. The codebase itself treats local credential events as audit-worthy: open registration goes through `register_open_user_with_audit` with a durable intent and compensating deletion (local.py:483-510), while admin-driven creation and reset of the same credentials go unaudited. Medium severity is right: this is a missing durable audit row, not an authorization bypass, because only administrators are admitted and they are already trusted.
verdicts.evidence: src/elspeth/web/auth/admin_routes.py:1-10 (the new docstring: 'Credential creation and reset retain their operational log events'). admin_routes.py:145-157: the `_require_local_account_admin` gate widened by ce3602aed. admin_routes.py:203 `_slog.info("dev_admin_user_created", ...)` and :220 `_slog.info("dev_admin_password_reset", ...)`: no audit call. local.py:451-481 create_user and :720-735 set_password: plain auth.db writes with no audit. By contrast, local.py:483+ `register_open_user_with_audit` does audit. identity_authority.py:1471-1482 `active_human_admin_ids`: the admission population. web/auth/audit.py record_* list (lines 200-526): no credential_created or password_reset event. Diff of ce3602aed: it removed 'Mutations are recorded via structlog only -- this surface is off in any deployment whose audit trail matters' and the config.py comment 'Short-term dev deployments only ... production deployments ... must leave this unset'. docs/specs/2026-09-02-pluggable-sso-design.md:969: 'structlog-only by design', premised on the dev-only gate. `git log 7c986dc97..74c0ce0db -- admin_routes.py audit.py` lists only ce3602aed and 793d0f95a; neither adds an audit event. No ruling in docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md (grep for credential/dev_admin/local account found nothing relevant).

findings.title: Deleting the configured dev admin's account frees a username that still grants credential administration
findings.summary: is_dev_admin grants local-account admin by username match. Since ce3602aed, any local admin may DELETE the dev admin's account; the only guard stops self-deletion. Nothing reserves the name. Under open registration (the default) a stranger can re-register it and inherit the grant. The UI's delete dialog promises that a later account with that name 'starts fresh'.
findings.failure_scenario: Settings: auth_provider=local, dev_admin_user=devadmin, registration_mode=open. Admin alice deletes 'devadmin'; the identity is retired and the name freed. An anonymous user POSTs /api/auth/register as 'devadmin' and is activated immediately (app.py:1118). is_dev_admin is now true, so they list every account, reset an administrator's password (unaudited, F1), sign in as that administrator and gain identity-admin authority.
findings.evidence: admin_routes.py:123-131 compares by username. admin_routes.py:235 blocks only user_id == admin.username. config.py:224 defaults registration_mode to 'open'. app.py:1118 activates on open registration. routes.py register has no reserved-name check. SignInSection.tsx:132 says 'A later account named X starts fresh. It does not receive this person's roles...'
findings.suggested_fix: Refuse deletion of the configured dev_admin_user account on the web surface, or bind the dev-admin grant to an identity_id rather than a reusable username. Reject registration of the configured dev_admin_user name.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this. I traced every step at 74c0ce0db and found no guard on the path.

1. The dev-admin grant is decided only by comparing the username with `dev_admin_user` (admin_routes.py:131). `can_manage_local_accounts` returns True on that match before it looks at any role (admin_routes.py:140-141).
2. Since ce3602aed, any active human admin passes `_require_local_account_admin`. Before that commit, only the dev admin did, and it could not delete itself. The web DELETE surface could therefore never remove the dev-admin account; now it can.
3. `delete_user` refuses only self-deletion (admin_routes.py:235) and `LastActiveAdminProtected`. The dev-admin grant does not depend on a role, so the dev-admin account need not be an administrator, and the last-admin rule does not protect it.
4. `LocalAuthProvider.delete_user` deletes the credential row. It retires the identity together with its natural key, so the next registration of that username gets a new identity (local.py:631-677).
5. Registration defaults to open (config.py:224). Open registration is refused only under `closed` (routes.py:371). It inserts the username with no reserved-name check (local.py:515-520). `_admit_identity` activates the new identity when `registration_mode == "open"` (app.py:1118).
6. The token's username is the local account name (local.py:1102, 1243). So `is_dev_admin` is true again for whoever registers the name, and they can list, create, delete and reset passwords for every local account. `reset_password` writes only a structlog line (admin_routes.py:217).
7. Nothing in `WebSettings._validate_auth_fields` (config.py:1084-1088) forbids combining `dev_admin_user` with open registration. docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md records no ruling on this.

Mitigating factors:
- An administrator has to act first by deleting that account.
- The same weakness already existed before the window: a configured `dev_admin_user` that was never created, or one removed with the CLI, can be claimed by anyone under open registration.
- The finding's severity (medium) stands. The new part is that an ordinary admin can now open the gap from the web UI, whose delete dialog (SignInSection.tsx:132) says a later account with that name 'starts fresh'. For the configured dev-admin name that is not true: it gets the credential-administration grant back.
verdicts.evidence:
- admin_routes.py:131: `return dev_admin_surface_enabled(settings) and user.username == settings.dev_admin_user`
- admin_routes.py:140-141: `if is_dev_admin(settings, user): return True`, checked before `active_human_admin_ids`.
- admin_routes.py:235: `if user_id == admin.username:` is the only guard apart from `LastActiveAdminProtected`.
- ce3602aed replaced `_require_dev_admin` with `_require_local_account_admin` on DELETE.
- local.py:631-677: `delete_user` deletes the credential, then retires the identity and its natural key ("a later registration of the same username gets a FRESH identity").
- local.py:515-520: open registration runs a plain INSERT and fails only on an IntegrityError for a duplicate name.
- routes.py:371: registration is refused only when `registration_mode == "closed"`.
- config.py:224: `registration_mode` defaults to `"open"`.
- app.py:1118: `activate=settings.registration_mode == "open"`.
- local.py:1102: `UserIdentity(user_id=identity_id, username=user_id)`, so the username is the local account name.
- config.py:1084-1088: no validation rule links `dev_admin_user` to `registration_mode`.
- admin_routes.py:217: a password reset is recorded only by `_slog.info`.
- SignInSection.tsx:132: "A later account named X starts fresh. It does not receive this person's roles, limits or history."

findings.title: 'Creating the account does not grant access' is false under the default open registration
findings.summary: An admin-created local account self-admits as ACTIVE on first sign-in when registration_mode is 'open' (the default), because ensure_identity is called with activate=registration_mode=='open'. The form tells the administrator that access still has to be set up, and PeopleCapabilities does not carry registration_mode, so the UI cannot tell which is true.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin creates an account for someone, intending to approve access later, and hands over the password. That person signs in and works immediately with the default quota, and no administrator ever set up access.
findings.evidence: local.py:1183 _login_sync calls _admitted_identity_id. local.py:1229 calls _admit, which calls the app.py:1116-1119 _admit_identity with activate=settings.registration_mode == 'open'. config.py:224 default is 'open'. Plan people-access-panel.md, 'Add a local person' step 4. ce3602aed widened the audience from the dev admin to all local identity admins.
findings.suggested_fix: Expose registration_mode (or an 'accounts self-admit' fact) in PeopleCapabilities and word the copy from it. Otherwise pre-provision the identity as pending when an admin creates the account.

verdicts.reason: The finding holds. The form's copy is false under the default open registration mode. Creating the account writes only the credential and never creates an identity row. On first sign-in, `_admitted_identity_id` calls `ensure_identity` with activate=(registration_mode=="open"), and "open" is the default. The new identity is therefore created ACTIVE and the person gets a working token without any administrator setting up access. Two parts of the finding are overstated. First, the UI can tell which is true: the public /api/auth/config response already carries registration_mode (routes.py:159, types/index.ts:26), even though PeopleCapabilities does not. Second, the practical impact is small. In open mode anyone can self-register and self-admit through /register anyway, so this does not bypass access control. The real harm is an administrator who believes they are gating access when they are not. I lowered the severity from medium to low. It is correctly marked diff_anchored=false: the copy dates from a767c7767, before the window. ce3602aed, inside the window, widened who sees it.
verdicts.evidence:
- AddPersonForm.tsx:105 (blame a767c7767, before the window) states "Creating the account does not grant access". Its createLocal (lines 62-75) calls only POST /api/auth/admin/users.
- admin_routes.py create_user (around lines 184-205) calls provider.create_user and nothing else. local.py:451-481 create_user only INSERTs into the auth.db users row, with email_verified defaulting to True. No identity row is pre-provisioned.
- local.py:1183: _login_sync returns _issue_token(self._admitted_identity_id(username)). local.py:1214-1236: _admitted_identity_id → _admit → admit_identity, and it raises AccessPending only when the record is not active.
- app.py:1110-1119: _admit_identity calls identity_authority.ensure_identity with activate=settings.registration_mode == "open". The comment there says open registration means "anyone may admit themselves".
- config.py:224: registration_mode defaults to "open".
- identity_authority.py:1544-1557: an existing pre-provisioned row outranks activate; otherwise a new row is created with the activate decision. So a new local account self-admits as active under open mode.
- Plan docs/plans/2026-09-20-people-access-panel.md:153-154 says "Do not pretend that creating the password grants access". The plan did not consider open mode, and no ruling in recent-code-hints covers this.
- Mitigating: routes.py:159 exposes registration_mode in AuthConfigResponse, and LoginPage.tsx:193/316 already consume it, so the "UI cannot tell" claim is wrong. Open mode already lets anyone self-register at /register (routes.py:371-381), so this is misleading copy, not an authorization bypass.
- ce3602aed ("let local administrators manage local accounts") is in the window 7c986dc97..74c0ce0db and widened who sees this copy.

findings.title: Unfinished-deletion recovery disappears after a reload, and the new comment claims a reload fallback
findings.summary: The comment added in 793d0f95a says the reason field is 'the ask-again fallback when none is held (a reload)'. Both `deleting` and `reason` are component state, so after a reload `deleting` is null, `unfinished` is false and the Finish-removal form never renders. The server still exposes the half-deleted state (provider local, local_account null, retired false, local_accounts true), but the UI offers no recovery, and line 82 tells the local account administrator that someone else manages local accounts.
findings.failure_scenario: The credential delete commits, then the retirement or audit transaction fails (reproduced in people-access-implementation-review.md §5). The admin closes or reopens the panel. The person is still live with their roles and no credential, and the UI shows no way to finish the removal. Under open registration, the next registration of that username binds to the live identity and inherits its roles, per local.py delete_user's own docstring; only the CLI can finish.
findings.evidence: SignInSection.tsx:39-44 declare useState-only deleting/reason and the new comment. :65 unfinished = account === null && deleting !== null && identityRetired === false. :82 copy. people_routes.py:223 manage_credentials = account is not None. local.py delete_user docstring on inherited identities.
findings.suggested_fix: Derive 'unfinished' from server state (provider local, no account, not retired, caller has local_accounts) and offer Finish removal with a reason field. Otherwise correct the comment and commit claim.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this finding. At 74c0ce0db the Finish-removal recovery depends entirely on component-local state. `deleting` is useState (SignInSection.tsx:39) and is set only by the delete-form submit (:124). `unfinished` is computed at :65 as `account === null && deleting !== null && identityRetired === false`. Nothing in the parent or the server can rebuild it: PersonDetail.tsx:206 passes only person.local_account, person.retired and actions.manage_credentials. On the server, manage_credentials is `account is not None` (people_routes.py:223), and the account lookup at :426 returns None once the credential is gone. So after a reload or a remount, a half-deleted person (provider local, local_account null, retired false) falls into the `account === null` branch. The form is never shown, and :82 says local accounts are managed by the local account administrator, which is the caller. The comment at :40-43 was added in window commit 793d0f95a. It calls the field 'the ask-again fallback when none is held (a reload)', and the commit message says 'asks again when none is held'. Both claims are false for the reload case. The empty-reason fallback is reachable only in a narrow same-mount sequence: the delete fails, the user presses Cancel, and cancelDelete clears the reason while `deleting` stays set. No UI path retires the identity: AccessSection offers only approve/enable/disable (:49). local.py delete_user's docstring (:650-671) confirms that the half-state lets the next registration of that username inherit the identity, and that a re-run of the removal is the intended recovery. Here only the CLI can do that re-run.

One caveat: the `deleting` useState and the reload blind spot existed before this window (in 793d0f95a's diff the `deleting` lines are unchanged context). What the window added is the false comment and the matching commit claim. The finding is still diff-anchored and correct. I kept medium because the half-state needs a failure between two commits, which is rare, and the CLI can recover. But the consequence, role inheritance by a later registrant, is authz-relevant, and the UI misleads the one admin who could act.
verdicts.evidence: SignInSection.tsx:39 `const [deleting, setDeleting] = useState<string | null>(null);`. :40-43 is the new comment ending 'is the ask-again fallback when none is held (a reload)'. :44 reason is useState(""). :65 `const unfinished = account === null && deleting !== null && identityRetired === false;`. :82 'Local accounts are managed by the local account administrator.' :124 is the only setDeleting call. PersonDetail.tsx:206 passes only account={person.local_account} identityRetired={person.retired} canManage={person.actions.manage_credentials}. people_routes.py:223 `manage_credentials=account is not None`. :426-430: the account read returns None when the credential is gone. AccessSection.tsx:49: the actions are only approve/enable/disable, with no retire. local.py:631-671 (delete_user docstring): a deleted credential with failed retirement means 'the next registration would inherit' the identity, and a re-run of the removal is the recovery. `git show 793d0f95a` shows the reason state and comment were added in the window, the `deleting` state was pre-existing context, and the commit message says 'The finish-removal retry sends the reason already typed and asks again when none is held.'

findings.title: Session-before-identity reorder deadlocks against provider-attempt admission (identity FOR UPDATE, then session FK KEY SHARE)
findings.summary: 89444b793 reordered progress writes and ticket issue/consume to lock the session row FOR UPDATE before the identity FOR UPDATE. SessionServiceImpl.begin_provider_attempt still does it the other way round. It takes only the session advisory lock, then assess locks identities FOR UPDATE (chargeable_admission_authority.py:39-43) while the session row stays unlocked, and then the quota_provider_attempts INSERT takes FOR KEY SHARE on the sessions row through its session_id FK (quota_authority.py:165, models.py:4039). The two orders form a cycle that did not exist before the window. The same pattern exists before the window in ReviewAuthority request/cancel/attest (engine.begin with no advisory lock, then session FOR UPDATE, then owner identity FOR UPDATE). settle_provider_attempt (ledger INSERT with identity and session FKs, no session row lock) probably forms the same cycle, depending on FK trigger order, which was not measured.
findings.failure_scenario: PostgreSQL deployment, run executing LLM calls on session S owned by X. Each call runs _admit_run_llm_call, then begin_provider_attempt: advisory(S), then identities X FOR UPDATE. The user opens or reconnects the run websocket, and ticket issue takes sessions S FOR UPDATE (free, because admission holds only the advisory lock) and then waits on X. The admission's INSERT INTO quota_provider_attempts needs FOR KEY SHARE on S, which conflicts with the ticket's FOR UPDATE. PostgreSQL raises 40P01 and aborts one side. Either the websocket ticket fails, or the audited run LLM call's before_call raises OperationalError and the call fails for an infrastructure reason. The same cycle occurs between the compose heartbeat (heartbeat_request every 15 s: session, then identity) and admit_provider_attempt for the same compose turn, which can fail the turn.
findings.evidence: composer_progress_authority.py:135-138,252-255,288-291,323-326 now take session FOR UPDATE, then identity FOR UPDATE (git show 89444b793). websocket_ticket_authority.py:47-55 and :105-113 take session FOR UPDATE, then identity FOR UPDATE. sessions/service.py:10501-10512: _session_process_locked_begin + _session_write_lock (advisory only, service.py:4801-4822) + _require_session_operation_context_on_connection (plain fence SELECT, :4931-4964), then begin_provider_attempt_on_connection. chargeable_admission_authority.py:36-43: unlocked session SELECT, then identities FOR UPDATE. quota_authority.py:163-177: unlocked session SELECT, then INSERT quota_provider_attempts (session_id FK to sessions.id). Callers: composer/provider_quota.py:110, sessions/_auto_title.py:343, execution/service.py:4358-4367 (LLMCallGovernance.before_call). The new test tests/testcontainer/web/test_composer_progress_quota_lock_order_postgres.py:103-110 covers only settlement, and its settle() pre-locks sessions FOR UPDATE. Before the window, progress and ticket took identity first, waited on admission's X while holding nothing admission needed, so there was no cycle.
findings.suggested_fix: Lock the session row before any identity lock in admission and settlement: add .with_for_update() to the session read in RepositoryChargeableAdmissionAuthority.assess (chargeable_admission_authority.py:36-38) and to settle_provider_attempt_on_connection's session read (quota_authority.py:189). Alternatively, route begin_provider_attempt and settle_provider_attempt through session_operation_authority.mutate, which locks the session row first. Add testcontainer cases for admission versus ticket issue and admission versus heartbeat. Update the progress docstring claim that writes 'match token accounting'.

verdicts.reason: I could not refute this. On PostgreSQL the claimed lock cycle can be reached with exactly the inputs the finding describes, and nothing earlier in either path guards against it. begin_provider_attempt holds only the session advisory lock, which the ticket and progress writers never take, so the sessions row stays unlocked. It then locks the owner identity FOR UPDATE and afterwards inserts a quota_provider_attempts row. That insert has an immediate (non-deferrable) foreign key to sessions.id, so it needs FOR KEY SHARE on the session row. Since 89444b793, ticket issue/consume and the progress writers (heartbeat_request, bind_request, publish, begin_request, replay, clear) lock sessions FOR UPDATE first and identity second. FOR UPDATE conflicts with FOR KEY SHARE, so the waits form a cycle: the ticket side holds S and waits for X, while admission holds X and waits for S. PostgreSQL then raises 40P01. Before the commit the ticket and progress writers locked identity first, so they never held S while waiting for X, and no cycle was possible. The new tests do not cover this path. The ticket test's session-fenced writer is modelled as a holder that locks sessions FOR UPDATE first, and admission never does that. The progress test uses record_token_usage_on_connection after pre-locking the session. Neither exercises begin_provider_attempt. docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md has no ruling on lock order or provider attempts. Severity stays high because a deadlock on the run side sends the database error out of LLMCallGovernance.before_call and into the provider call. I did not trace the retry path in full, and the timing window (from the identity lock to the INSERT) is narrow, so frequency is low but real. I did not confirm the settlement leg, which the finding itself marks as unmeasured, because it depends on which foreign-key trigger fires first.
verdicts.evidence:
Admission side (no row lock on sessions):
- sessions/service.py:10501-10512: `_session_process_locked_begin` (PostgreSQL: a plain `engine.begin`, per sessions/locking.py:248-252) plus `_session_write_lock` (advisory lock only, service.py:4801-4822), then the fence check. `_require_session_operation_context_on_connection` (service.py:4931-4964) is a plain SELECT on session_operation_fences.
- chargeable_admission_authority.py:36-38: unlocked `select(sessions_table...)`. Lines 39-43: `identities ... .with_for_update()`.
- quota_authority.py:163-177: `INSERT quota_provider_attempts(session_id=fence.session_id, ...)`.
- models.py:4039: `ForeignKey("sessions.id", ondelete="RESTRICT")`, not deferrable. The only deferrable FK is models.py:1333, on a different table. PostgreSQL's foreign-key check locks the parent row FOR KEY SHARE.

Ticket and progress side after 89444b793:
- websocket_ticket_authority.py:47-55 (issue) and :105-113 (consume): `.with_for_update(of=sessions_table)` on the session, then identities FOR UPDATE.
- The SQLAlchemy PostgreSQL compiler (sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/base.py:2138-2141) emits plain ` FOR UPDATE` when `key_share` is not set, and FOR UPDATE conflicts with FOR KEY SHARE.
- composer_progress_authority.py:252-255 (heartbeat_request): session first, then identity. The same order holds at :135-138, :288-291 and :323-326.
- The `git show 89444b793` diff shows the old order was identity first, then session.

Reachability:
- app.py:1776-1780 wires RepositorySessionWebsocketTicketAuthority and DatabaseComposerProgressRegistry only when the dialect is postgresql.
- execution/routes.py:2058 issues tickets for a run.
- execution/service.py:3657 and :4358-4367 call begin_provider_attempt for each run LLM call. The gateway (gateway.py:594) calls `before_call()` with no try around it.

Test gaps:
- tests/testcontainer/web/test_cross_process_ticket_postgres.py (added in 89444b793): the holder locks sessions FOR UPDATE first.
- test_composer_progress_quota_lock_order_postgres.py:103-110: settle() pre-locks the session and uses record_token_usage_on_connection.
- No testcontainer test pits begin_provider_attempt against a ticket or a heartbeat.

Rulings: `grep` over docs/agents/recent-code-hints.md for lock order, KEY SHARE, provider_attempt and 89444b793 returned nothing.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the lock cycle. I traced it at 74c0ce0db and it is real, and 89444b793, inside the window, introduced it. No recorded ruling covers it. The commit says it reorders progress, ticket and approval locks 'session before identity to match token-ledger settlement'. That is true for settlement, but provider-attempt admission still locks the identity row first and only then touches the session row, through the INSERT's foreign-key check. Nothing serializes the two sides. Admission holds only the session advisory lock, which ticket issue/consume and progress heartbeat/publish never take. No code under src/elspeth/web handles 40P01 or DeadlockDetected, and no testcontainer test puts begin_provider_attempt against ticket issue or heartbeat.

I am lowering the severity from high to medium. In this cycle the session-first transaction (ticket, consume or heartbeat) always starts waiting first, because it blocks on identity X, which admission already holds. PostgreSQL's deadlock check runs in the waiter whose deadlock_timeout expires first, so that side is normally the one aborted. Every one of those victims recovers. A ticket-issue 500 reaches websocket.ts:132-148, which calls scheduleReconnect with backoff. A consume error before accept fails the handshake, which the client treats as 1006 and reconnects. A heartbeat OperationalError is retried at _helpers.py:2546-2552. The admission itself stalls for about deadlock_timeout (1 s by default) and then goes ahead. The finding's worse outcome, the audited run LLM call failing, is not the expected victim. This victim selection comes from PostgreSQL's documented behaviour and was not measured, because running tests was out of scope. What remains is a real regression: spurious 40P01 errors, websocket reconnect churn and roughly 1 s admission stalls, all likely under load because admission transactions on a busy run follow each other almost continuously. It is not a failure path for audited calls.
verdicts.evidence:
Pinned worktree the pinned review worktree at 74c0ce0db.

- **Ticket side, changed in the window.** websocket_ticket_authority.py:47-55 (issue) and :105-113 (consume) lock sessions FOR UPDATE (of=sessions), then identities FOR UPDATE. `git show 89444b793` shows these were identity-first before the commit. 89444b793 is in the range 7c986dc97..74c0ce0db.
- **Admission side, unchanged.** sessions/service.py:10501-10510: begin_provider_attempt calls _session_process_locked_begin and then _session_write_lock. On PostgreSQL that lock is advisory only (service.py:4801-4822). The fence check is a plain SELECT (:4950-4960). Then chargeable_admission_authority.py:36-43 reads sessions with no lock and locks identities FOR UPDATE. After that, quota_authority.py:163-177 does INSERT INTO quota_provider_attempts, and its session_id column is a ForeignKey to sessions.id (models.py:4039). In PostgreSQL that foreign-key check takes FOR KEY SHARE on the sessions row, which conflicts with FOR UPDATE. Nothing on the admission side locks the session row before identity X.
- **The cycle.** Admission locks X, then the ticket locks S and waits on X, then admission's INSERT waits on S. That is a deadlock.
- **Progress side, same pattern.** composer_progress_authority.py:250-255 (heartbeat) and the bind/publish paths take session FOR UPDATE, then identity FOR UPDATE, with no advisory lock.
- **No handling.** Grepping src/elspeth/web for 40P01, DeadlockDetected and SerializationFailure returns nothing.
- **Tests.** tests/testcontainer/web/test_composer_progress_quota_lock_order_postgres.py:103-110 exercises only settlement, and its settle() locks sessions FOR UPDATE first. No testcontainer test pairs begin_provider_attempt with ticket issue or heartbeat.
- **Why the victims recover.** frontend/src/api/websocket.ts:132-148 retries a non-401/404 ticket-fetch failure through scheduleReconnect. execution/routes.py:1635 calls consume before websocket.accept(), so a consume error fails the handshake (seen as 1006) and the client reconnects. sessions/routes/_helpers.py:2546-2552 retries a heartbeat OperationalError while the lease still has headroom.
- **Why admission is normally not the victim.** The ticket or heartbeat side begins waiting first, so its deadlock_timeout fires first and it aborts itself. This is PostgreSQL's documented behaviour and was not measured here.

findings.title: Prompt review for a multi-query llm node without a node-level prompt_template is permanently unapprovable
findings.summary: The window's gate `approveGated = requiresPromptView && (!promptReviewAvailable || ...)` blocks Approve whenever resolvePromptDisplaySegments returns reviewAvailable:false. The frontend multiQuerySurfaceFromOptions (promptTemplateDisplay.ts:192) requires a string prompt_template. The backend multi_query_prompt_surface_from_options (interpretation_state.py:2706-2717) admits an absent/None node-level template, and an inline-blob marker when every query is templated. It stages and surfaces an llm_prompt_template review for these nodes, and the frontend can never render or approve it.
findings.failure_scenario: The composer authors an llm node with queries {a:{template:...}, b:{template:...}}, a system_prompt and no node-level prompt_template. The new _validate_llm_prompt_roles_present admits this, and LLMConfig's rule as restated at state.py:3805 does too. _options_with_default_prompt_template_review stages a pending PT requirement from surface.render_for_review(). _missing_prompt_template_review_sites enumerates the site and a pending event is written. On the card, resolvePromptDisplaySegments falls through to reviewAvailable:false, so Approve stays aria-disabled forever with 'Reload the session…' copy that cannot help. supportsAmendment is false for llm_prompt_template, so there is no Change… path. The pending review blocks execution, and the only exit is opting out of all reviews for the session. At 7c986dc97 the same card fell back to llm_draft and was approvable after View prompt.
findings.evidence: AcknowledgementCard.tsx:419 and :729 (07faf477e); promptTemplateDisplay.ts:184-195 and :333-337; interpretation_state.py:2706-2717 skips the guard when prompt_template is None; render_for_review 2466-2471 handles node_prompt_template=None; _missing_prompt_template_review_sites 1646-1670; tools/_common.py:383-420. `git diff --stat 7c986dc97 74c0ce0db -- interpretation_state.py` is empty, so the producer did not change and the gate is the regression. promptTemplateDisplay.test.ts:543-554 wrongly asserts 'the backend reads no surface'.
findings.suggested_fix: Make multiQuerySurfaceFromOptions admit exactly what the backend admits: an absent/null prompt_template, and a marker when every query has a template. Render the node-level template as 'not used'. Fix the backend docstrings at interpretation_state.py:2689 and 1638-1641.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this. I traced the path at 74c0ce0db and every step holds.

- **The node is admitted.** LLMConfig types `prompt_template` as `str | None` and requires it only when some query has no template (plugins/transforms/llm/base.py:219, :435). The window's `_validate_llm_prompt_roles_present` (composer/state.py:3829-3844) accepts a node where every query has a template and there is no node-level `prompt_template`.
- **The backend stages the review.** `multi_query_prompt_surface_from_options` (interpretation_state.py:2703-2717) accepts a missing or None `prompt_template`, and an inline blob marker when every query has a template. `prompt_review_draft_from_options` (:2850-2852) then returns `render_for_review()`, and `_options_with_default_prompt_template_review` (tools/_common.py:407-420) stages a pending requirement.
- **The backend writes and can resolve the event.** `_missing_prompt_template_review_sites` (:1648-1649) enumerates the site. The service auto-surfacer (service.py:2030-2043) returns the rendered surface as the draft. `create_pending_interpretation_event` (pending_interpretation.py:1956-1959) and the resolver (:1175-1178) both explicitly accept a non-string `prompt_template` when the multi-query surface is not None.
- **The frontend cannot render it.** `multiQuerySurfaceFromOptions` (promptTemplateDisplay.ts:187-195) returns null unless `prompt_template` is a string. `segmentsFromParts(undefined)` returns null (:92), and the `typeof template === "string"` branch is skipped. So `resolvePromptDisplaySegments` reaches the final branch, which returns `reviewAvailable: false` (:333-337).
- **Approve stays blocked.** In AcknowledgementCard.tsx, `approveGated = requiresPromptView && (!promptReviewAvailable || ...)` (:419) is true whether or not the prompt has been viewed. The Approve click returns early, and the gate note (:728-729) tells the user to reload, which changes nothing.
- **This is new in the window.** Before 07faf477e, `PromptDisplayResult` had no `reviewAvailable` field. That commit added the field and the `!promptReviewAvailable` gate. At 7c986dc97 the card fell back to `llm_draft` and could be approved after View prompt.
- **It is not a recorded ruling.** docs/reviews/2026-09-22-chat-card-repairs.md:9-11 aims to stop a bounded preview from being approved while the composition is still loading. It does not mention this node shape, and recent-code-hints.md has no entry for it.

Two parts of the finding are wrong:
- **The test is correct.** The test at promptTemplateDisplay.test.ts:543-554 uses `prompt_template: 7`, and the backend returns None for that value too (not None, not a string, not a marker). The missing coverage is a test for an absent `prompt_template`.
- **There is an exit.** The user or planner can add any node-level `prompt_template`. It would be listed as unused, but it makes the frontend surface non-null. The card is therefore not permanently unapprovable.

Given that exit, I rate it medium rather than high. It still blocks execution of a valid config, and the on-screen advice to reload does not help.
verdicts.evidence:
All citations are to the worktree at 74c0ce0db.

**Frontend gate**
- promptTemplateDisplay.ts:187-195 has the string-only check, `typeof promptTemplate !== "string"` → return null.
- promptTemplateDisplay.ts:333-337 is the fallback that returns `reviewAvailable: false`.
- AcknowledgementCard.tsx:391 sets `promptReviewAvailable = promptDisplay?.reviewAvailable === true`.
- AcknowledgementCard.tsx:419 sets `approveGated = requiresPromptView && (!promptReviewAvailable || (!promptViewed && !expanded))`.
- AcknowledgementCard.tsx:728-729 shows the gate note "Reload the session if it does not load; the preview cannot be approved."
- `git diff 7c986dc97 74c0ce0db -- promptTemplateDisplay.ts` shows `reviewAvailable` was added in the window by 07faf477e. It is the only window commit touching AcknowledgementCard.tsx, promptTemplateDisplay.ts or interpretation_state.py.

**Backend admits and surfaces the node**
- interpretation_state.py:2711-2718: a None template skips the guard, and a blob marker is accepted when every query has a template. `git blame` dates these lines to 9a02bac8f4 (2026-09-15), before the window.
- interpretation_state.py:1648-1649 enumerates the review site.
- interpretation_state.py:2850-2852 produces the draft from the rendered surface.
- tools/_common.py:407-420 stages the pending requirement.
- service.py:2030-2043 surfaces the card.
- pending_interpretation.py:1956-1959 (writer) and :1175-1178 (resolver) accept a non-string `prompt_template` when the surface is not None.

**The config is valid**
- base.py:219 and :435: `prompt_template` is required only when some query has no template.
- state.py:3829-3844: `llm_user_prompt_missing` fires only for a query with no template.

**Where the finding overstates**
- promptTemplateDisplay.test.ts:543-554 uses `prompt_template: 7`. The backend also returns None for that value, so the test is correct.

verdicts.reason: I could not refute this. I traced the failure path myself at 74c0ce0db. For a multi-query llm node that has per-query templates and no node-level prompt_template, the backend stages, surfaces, writes and can resolve an llm_prompt_template review. At 07faf477e the frontend began requiring reviewAvailable before Approve. The frontend's multi-query parser rejects this shape, so the card ends with reviewAvailable:false and Approve is permanently aria-disabled. No recorded ruling covers it. The composer skill teaches exactly this shape ("one user prompt per query (queries.<name>.template)"), so the path is reachable. Before the window, the gate was `requiresPromptView && !promptViewed`, so the card showed the llm_draft fallback and could be approved after View prompt. That makes this a regression introduced in the window. There are workarounds: asking the composer in chat to add a node-level prompt_template, or opting out of reviews. Neither is discoverable, and the gate note ("Reload the session…") points the user at something that cannot help. High severity stands. One part of the finding is wrong: promptTemplateDisplay.test.ts:543-554 uses prompt_template: 7. The backend also returns None for that shape (it is not a blob marker), so that test's comment is correct. This does not affect the main defect.
verdicts.evidence:
Frontend, pinned:
- promptTemplateDisplay.ts:184-195: multiQuerySurfaceFromOptions returns null when `typeof promptTemplate !== "string"`.
- resolvePromptDisplaySegments (~:305-337): segmentsFromParts(undefined) returns null because of `!Array.isArray(raw)` at :92. options.prompt_template is not a string, so it falls through to `{segments: llm_draft, reviewAvailable: false}`.
